summary:
SPHEREx Time Machine is an interactive web application that helps users explore how objects and regions of the sky change over time using open data from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. We developed an accessible platform that retrieves real SPHEREx observations, processes scientific FITS images, and allows users to compare observations from different dates and infrared wavelength bands through Blink, Swipe, Difference, Movie, and Side-by-Side modes.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming complex astronomical archives into a clear visual experience. Users can explore verified sky targets, including the Orion Nebula, Andromeda Galaxy, Pleiades, and Galactic Center, and use AI-assisted analysis to identify potential changes, estimate confidence, explain supporting evidence, and highlight limitations.

This is important because astronomical data is often difficult to access without specialist knowledge and software. SPHEREx Time Machine makes NASA data more understandable for students, educators, citizen scientists, and researchers while demonstrating how human exploration and responsible AI can work together to investigate our changing universe.
details:
SPHEREx Time Machine is an interactive web application that allows users to explore how objects and regions of the sky change over time using real observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Users can select a location on an interactive sky map, search by object name or coordinates, or choose one of seven verified demonstration targets. The application finds available SPHEREx exposures, processes the scientific FITS data, aligns the images on a common sky grid, and allows users to compare observations from different dates and infrared wavelengths.

The project offers five comparison modes: Blink, Swipe, Difference, Movie, and Side-by-Side. It also includes AI-assisted change analysis powered by Google Gemini. The AI examines two selected frames, their difference image, and calculated signal measurements. It then provides a possible classification, confidence level, supporting evidence, limitations, and recommended next steps. These results are presented as preliminary interpretations rather than confirmed scientific discoveries.

The main benefit of the project is accessibility. Astronomical archives normally require specialist knowledge, scientific software, and experience with FITS files and celestial coordinates. SPHEREx Time Machine brings these steps together in a clear browser-based interface, making NASA data easier to explore for students, educators, citizen scientists, astronomy enthusiasts, and researchers.

The application was developed using Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, Pillow, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Aladin Lite provides the interactive sky map. The project uses SPHEREx data from NASA/IPAC IRSA and NASA’s public AWS Open Data bucket. It also integrates the JPL Small-Body Identification service to identify known asteroids and comets. The application is deployed on Vercel, while the source code is stored on GitHub. API keys are securely stored as server-side environment variables and are never exposed in the browser or public repository.

A creative feature of the project is its “time machine” approach to astronomical data. Instead of showing a single static image, it turns repeated observations into an interactive visual investigation. The application automatically matches observations at similar wavelengths, aligns frames pixel by pixel, and produces difference images in which unchanged stars are reduced while possible changes become more visible.

During development, our team considered scientific accuracy, data availability, performance, security, usability, wavelength differences, image noise, saturation, alignment errors, detector artifacts, and cloud-platform time limits. Because arbitrary full-sky searches can sometimes take too long, the current MVP includes seven verified targets that provide reliable results during demonstrations. The intended impact is to make space science more understandable and participatory, while creating a foundation for future citizen-science tools that could help identify variable stars, moving objects, transient events, and other potentially interesting changes in the universe.
